Filtrations on 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules and multiplicities of roots of Bernstein-Sato polynomials

András C. Lőrincz and Ruijie Yang
Abstract.

In this paper, we relate multiplicities of Bernstein–Sato-type polynomials with respect to a function ff to several singularity invariants. First, we introduce certain “mod” bb-functions and show that they characterize the weight filtration on the localization of a simple algebraic holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module along ff, and we provide an algorithm to compute them. Second, we show that they can be approximated by the multiplicities of roots of power bb-functions (i.e., the bb-functions with respect to powers of ff). Furthermore, we give a sharp upper bound for the Hodge level of elements given by a certain sum of such multiplicities. Next, we give an effective asymptotic solution to the Gelfand problem by determining an explicit threshold after which every integer shift of a root of bf​(s)b_{f}(s) is a pole of the Archimedean zeta function of ff. We also show that the order of these poles is equal to the nilpotency index of the logarithmic monodromy operator, which we further express as the limit of the multiplicities of roots of power bb-functions. We define several filtrations, relating them to the weight and Hodge filtrations, based upon which we leave some open questions that we address in the affirmative in the case when ff has a homogeneous isolated singularity, or it is a hyperplane arrangement, or a semi-invariant on a spherical variety. We give several immediate applications to our results, including a solution to a question of Torrelli on whether 1/f1/f lies in the intersection complex of the hypersurface of ff if and only if −1-1 is a simple root of bf​(s)b_{f}(s).

1. Introduction

Let ff be a non-invertible regular (algebraic) function on a smooth complex algebraic variety XX. The Bernstein-Sato polynomial of ff is the unique monic polynomial b⁡(s)b(s) of smallest degree satisfying

P⁡(s)⋅fs+1=b⁡(s)​fs,for some P​(s)∈𝒟X​[s].P(s)\cdot f^{s+1}=b(s)f^{s},\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{for some $P(s)\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]$}.

While the roots of b⁡(s)b(s) carry a lot of geometric information, their multiplicities have been considered rather mysterious until now. In this paper, we systematically study the multiplicities of roots of various Bernstein-Sato-type polynomials and elucidate their meaning by relating them to singularity invariants of ff.

First, let ℳ=𝒮f≠0\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{S}_{f}\neq 0 be the localization of a simple holonomic (algebraic) 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module 𝒮\mathcal{S} along {f=0}\{f=0\}. We compute its weight filtration, which is induced by the mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module structure on ℳ\mathcal{M}, elementwise in terms of a certain “mod (s+α)ℓ(s+\alpha)^{\ell}” bb-function with respect to fkf^{k} for k≫0k\gg 0 (Corollary 1.7), and we provide an algorithm to compute it. Next, we study the limit of the multiplicities of the bb-functions of fkf^{k} as kk goes to infinity, and we relate this limit to the VV-filtration (Theorem 1.1) and the weight filtration (Theorem 1.3). If α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}, we express the nilpotency index nαn_{\alpha} of the logarithmic monodromy operator on the nearby and vanishing cycles of 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X} along ff in terms of the multiplicity of the bb-function of fkf^{k} for k≫0k\gg 0 (Corollary 1.9). This approach applies similarly to general 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules of the form ℳ=𝒮f\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{S}_{f} (Theorem 1.8). We also solve Gelfand’s problem up to finitely many exceptions by determining all poles of the Archimedean zeta function ZfZ_{f} and their exact orders (Theorem 1.11). We also answer a question of Torrelli regarding when 1/f1/f lies in the intersection complex of {f=0}\{f=0\} (Theorem 1.13).

1.1. Power bb-functions and pp-functions

Let us begin by an elementary discussion about multiplicities of bb-functions. Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module on which ff acts bijectively. For an element m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} and an integer k∈ℤ≥1k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, we define the kk-th power bb-function, denoted by bm(k)​(s)b_{m}^{(k)}(s), to be the unique monic polynomial in ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] of minimal degree for which there exists an operator P∈𝒟⁡[s]P\in\mathscr{D}[s] satisfying

(1) P⋅m​fs+k=bm(k)​(s)​m​fs.P\cdot mf^{s+k}=b_{m}^{(k)}(s)mf^{s}.

While it is easy to see that bm(k)​(k​s)b^{(k)}_{m}(ks) agrees with the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of mm with respect to fkf^{k} (see Definition 3.1), up to a constant, we intentionally choose this formulation to track the behavior of multiplicities for a fixed root. For instance, in Lemma 3.10, we show that

(2) lcm⁡(bm​(s),bm​(s+1),…,bm​(s+k−1))|bm(k)​(s)​∣bm(k+1)​(s)∣​∏i=0kbm​(s+i).\mathrm{lcm}\left(\,b_{m}(s),b_{m}(s+1),\dots,b_{m}(s+k-1)\,\right)\,\mid\,b_{m}^{(k)}(s)\mid b_{m}^{(k+1)}(s)\mid\prod_{i=0}^{k}b_{m}(s+i).

It immediately follows that for all k≥2k\geq 2, the roots of bm(k)​(s)b_{m}^{(k)}(s) are completely determined by the roots of the standard bb-function bm​(s)=bm(1)​(s)b_{m}(s)=b_{m}^{(1)}(s); this is also implicit in [11, Theorem 4.6].

The multiplicities of these roots, however, turn out to be rather interesting invariants. From the divisibility relations in (2), we observe that for a fixed α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, the sequence {mults=−α⁡bm(k)​(s)}k≥1\{\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{m}^{(k)}(s)\}_{k\geq 1} is non-decreasing and bounded above a constant depending only on bm​(s)b_{m}(s) and α\alpha. Consequently, limk→∞mults=−α⁡bm(k)​(s)\lim_{k\to\infty}\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{m}^{(k)}(s) must exist and we set

νm,α:⁣=limk→∞mults=−αbm(k)(s).\nu_{m,\alpha}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\lim_{k\to\infty}\mult_{s=-\alpha}b^{(k)}_{m}(s).

Our first main result is to reinterpret νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha} in terms of the VV-filtration. Fix α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C} and m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}. Let ι:X→X×ℂ\iota:X\to X\times\mathbb{C} be the graph embedding of ff sending xx to (x,f⁡(x))(x,f(x)). The pp-function pm,α​(s)p_{m,\alpha}(s) is defined as the unique monic polynomial in ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] of minimal degree satisfying

pm,α​(s)​m​fs∈Vα​ι+​ℳ,p_{m,\alpha}(s)mf^{s}\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M},

where V∙​ι+​ℳV^{\bullet}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} is the Kashiwara-Malgrange VV-filtration on ι+​ℳ\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} along the coordinate function on ℂ\mathbb{C} (see §2.1). Intuitively, because m​fs∈Vβ​ι+​ℳmf^{s}\in V^{\beta}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} for some β\beta, this polynomial measures precisely how far the element m​fsmf^{s} is from landing inside Vα​ι+​ℳV^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}. This notion first appeared in [34, Definition 2.11] and we give a systematic treatment in §3.3. Among them, we show that pm,α​(s)p_{m,\alpha}(s) exists (Lemma 3.14) and that pm,α​(−α)≠0p_{m,\alpha}(-\alpha)\neq 0. In Corollary 3.27 and Theorem 3.29, we establish the following relationships between νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha} and pp-functions.

Theorem 1.1.

For α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C} and 0≠m∈ℳ0\neq m\in\mathcal{M}, we have an equality

νm,α=mults=−α⁡bpm,α​(s)​m​fs​(s),\nu_{m,\alpha}=\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{p_{m,\alpha}(s)mf^{s}}(s),

where the limit stabilizes for k≥min⁡{k0∈ℤ>0∣bm​(−α+K)≠0​ for every K≥k0}k\geq\min\{k_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\mid b_{m}(-\alpha+K)\neq 0\textrm{ for every $K\geq k_{0}$}\}. Conversely, endowing ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with the lexicographic ordering, we have a finite product

pm,α​(s)=∏β<α(s+β)νm,β.p_{m,\alpha}(s)=\prod_{\beta<\alpha}(s+\beta)^{\nu_{m,\beta}}.

From now on, let us assume ℳ=𝒮f≠0\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{S}_{f}\neq 0, the localization of 𝒮\mathcal{S} along {f=0}\{f=0\}, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a simple holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module. While the pp-function plays a critical role in explicitly computing the VV-filtration in the equivariant setup of [34], we show that in general it serves as a powerful approximation for the weight level of elements in ℳ\mathcal{M}, as well as the Hodge levels if 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies a pure Hodge module.

We first explain how to put a weight filtration on ℳ=𝒮f\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{S}_{f}. Recall that (𝒪X)f(\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f} underlies a mixed Hodge module on XX by Saito’s theory [46]. It thus carries a weight filtration, which is traditionally of great interest for computing Deligne’s weight filtration on the singular cohomology of the open complement X∖{f=0}X\setminus\{f=0\} [20]. The theory of twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules of Sabbah [45] and Mochizuki [37] allows us to work in the generality where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a simple holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module. By the foundational work [37], 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies a polarizable, purely imaginary (wild) pure twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module on XX. For any α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, in §2.2 we show that ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} underlies a mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module in the sense of [38] and hence it is equipped with a canonical weight filtration (up to shifts) whose associated graded pieces are semi-simple 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules, by Mochizuki’s solution of Kashiwara’s conjecture and Lemma 2.10. Note that if 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies a (complex) pure Hodge module, then this weight filtration is determined by the theory of (complex) mixed Hodge modules [43, 46].

Now, let us explain how to approximate weight levels of elements in ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} using the numbers νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha}. This connection emerges naturally from our attempt to compute the weight filtration on ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} via the VV-filtration. More precisely, evaluation at s=−αs=-\alpha induces a surjective map

e​vs=−α:ι+​ℳ→∼ℳ⁡[s]​fs→s=−αℳ⋅f−α.ev_{s=-\alpha}\colon\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s}\xrightarrow{s=-\alpha}\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}.

The first 𝒟X​[s]\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]-isomorphism was observed by Malgrange [35] (see also Mustaţă–Popa [41]). In Theorem 4.1, we show that this map restricts to a surjective map

(3) e​vs=−α:Vα​ι+​ℳ→ℳ⋅f−α,ev_{s=-\alpha}\colon V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha},

which admits a set-theoretic section given by the pp-function: m​f−α↦pm,α​(s)pm,α​(−α)​m​fsmf^{-\alpha}\mapsto\frac{p_{m,\alpha}(s)}{p_{m,\alpha}(-\alpha)}mf^{s}.

For any element w∈Vα​ι+​ℳw\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, Sabbah’s Theorem [44] ensures that all roots of bw​(s)b_{w}(s) are bounded above by −α-\alpha. This property naturally gives rise to a filtration of coherent 𝒟X​⟨s,t⟩\mathscr{D}_{X}\langle s,t\rangle-modules on Vα​ι+​ℳV^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} (Proposition 4.10):

ZℓVαι+ℳ:⁣={w∈Vαι+ℳ∣mults=−αbw(s)≤ℓ},if ℓ∈ℤ≥0,Z_{\ell}V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{w\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\mid\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{w}(s)\leq\ell\},\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{if $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$},

see [13] for a related discussion. Using this, we prove the following result.

Proposition 1.2 (Theorem 4.15).

For any ℓ∈ℤ≥0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, we have an exact sequence

0→Zℓ+1​Vα​ι+​ℳ→s+αZℓ​Vα​ι+​ℳ→e​vs=−αWq+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)→0,0\to Z_{\ell+1}V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\xrightarrow{s+\alpha}Z_{\ell}V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\xrightarrow{ev_{s=-\alpha}}W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})\to 0,

where W∙W_{\bullet} is the weight filtration induced by the mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module structure on ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is pure of weight qq.

In particular, denote by ωm,α\omega_{m,\alpha} the weight level of m​f−αmf^{-\alpha} in ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}, i.e., the smallest integer ℓ\ell such that m​f−α∈Wq+ℓ​(ℳ​f−α)∖Wq+ℓ−1​(ℳ​f−α)mf^{-\alpha}\in W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}f^{-\alpha})\setminus W_{q+\ell-1}(\mathcal{M}f^{-\alpha}). Combined with Theorem 1.1, we have the following approximation.

Theorem 1.3.

For any m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, one has ωm,α≤νm,α\omega_{m,\alpha}\leq\nu_{m,\alpha}.

Although in many cases we find that ωm,α=νm,α\omega_{m,\alpha}=\nu_{m,\alpha} (see §6.5 and (9)), they do not agree in general. One subtle reason for this discrepancy is that, while the set {m​f−α∣νm,α≤ℓ}\{mf^{-\alpha}\mid\nu_{m,\alpha}\leq\ell\} always forms an 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-submodule of the 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module Wq+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) (Proposition 5.15), Lemma 5.21 provides examples where it fails to be a 𝒟\mathscr{D}-submodule. Nevertheless, we can ask whether this equality holds “generically”, after resolving this discrepancy.

Question 1.4.

Do we always have Wq+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)=𝒟X⋅{m​f−α∣νm,α≤ℓ}W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot\{mf^{-\alpha}\mid\nu_{m,\alpha}\leq\ell\}?

We answer this in the affirmative for certain values of ℓ\ell (e.g. see Proposition 5.19) and for some specific cases, such as when ff has an isolated quasi-homogeneous singularity, or it is a hyperplane arrangement (and 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}), or a semi-invariant on a spherical variety (see §6.5). In these examples we illustrate how the mechanism of our invariants ν\nu can be used effectively to calculate weight levels of various elements, such as powers of ff.

Suppose 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies a (complex) pure Hodge module [43], then ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} underlies a (complex) mixed Hodge module for α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} (see [16, §5] for example) and hence it carries a canonical Hodge filtration F∙F_{\bullet} starting at degree 00. In the case 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}, we find that the Hodge level of elements in ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} can be approximated using the degree of the pp-function.

Theorem 1.5.

Assume 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}, then for any m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, we have

m​f−α∈Fdeg⁡pm,α​(s)​(ℳ⋅f−α).mf^{-\alpha}\in F_{\deg p_{m,\alpha}(s)}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}).

In other words, the Hodge level of m​f−αmf^{-\alpha} is at most deg⁡pm,α​(s)=∑β<ανm,β\deg p_{m,\alpha}(s)=\sum_{\beta<\alpha}\nu_{m,\beta}.

In Section 6.5, we demonstrate that this containment is sharp in a number of cases, i.e. the Hodge level of m​f−αmf^{-\alpha} is equal to deg⁡pm,α​(s)\deg p_{m,\alpha}(s).

1.2. Weight filtration and (mod) bb-functions

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a simple holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module and ℳ=𝒮f\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{S}_{f}. By the discussion above, 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies a pure twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module, which we assume has weight qq and hence ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} is equipped with a weight filtration. Via Beilinson’s glueing formula, Saito [46] (in the Hodge case) and Mochizuki [38] showed that this weight filtration is ultimately controlled by the monodromy weight filtration on the nearby and vanishing cycles of ℳ\mathcal{M}.

The next result of our work captures the weight level of a given element in ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} via a relaxed functional equation utilizing bb-function-type invariants, which is inspired by Sabbah’s characterization of the VV-filtration [44] via bb-functions of elements.

Since ff acts bijectively on ℳ\mathcal{M}, there is a natural 𝒟X​[s]\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]-module structure on ℳ⁡[s]​fs\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s} [35] (see also [30]). For any element m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} and each integer k>0k>0, we define ℓm,k\ell_{m,k} as the minimal non-negative integer ℓ\ell such that there exists some P∈𝒟X​[s]P\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s] satisfying the congruence

(4) P⋅m​fs+k≡(s+α)ℓ​m​fs(mod(s+α)ℓ+1⋅ℳ⁡[s]​fs).P\cdot mf^{s+k}\equiv(s+\alpha)^{\ell}mf^{s}\pmod{(s+\alpha)^{\ell+1}\cdot\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s}}.

The sequence ℓm,k\ell_{m,k} stabilizes (Proposition 5.4), and considering the limit we obtain the following description of the weight level (recall that ωm,α\omega_{m,\alpha} is the weight level of m​f−αmf^{-\alpha})

(5) limk→∞ℓm,k=ωm,α.\lim_{k\to\infty}\ell_{m,k}=\omega_{m,\alpha}.

More precisely, we have the following (see Theorem 5.5 and Remark 5.6).

Theorem 1.6.

Take any 0≠m~∈ℳ0\neq\tilde{m}\in\mathcal{M} such that bm~​(s)b_{\tilde{m}}(s) has no roots in −α+ℤ≥0-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Then ωm,α\omega_{m,\alpha} is the minimal integer ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 satisfying

P⋅m~​fs=(s+α)ℓ​m​fs(mod(s+α)ℓ+1⋅ℳ⁡[s]​fs)P\cdot\tilde{m}f^{s}=(s+\alpha)^{\ell}mf^{s}\pmod{(s+\alpha)^{\ell+1}\cdot\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s}}

for some P∈𝒟X​[s]P\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]. In particular,

(6) ωm,α=ℓm,k, for any ​k>max⁡{j∈ℤ≥0∣bm​(−α+j)=0}.\omega_{m,\alpha}=\ell_{m,k},\,\,\mbox{ for any }k>\max\bigl\{j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\mid b_{m}(-\alpha+j)=0\bigr\}.

Based on this, we can deduce the following characterization of the weight filtration.

Corollary 1.7.

For any ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z} and α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C} we have a set-theoretic equality

Wq+ℓ(ℳ⋅f−α)={mf−α∣ℓm,k≤ℓ, for all k∈ℤ>0}.W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\{mf^{-\alpha}\mid\ell_{m,k}\leq\ell,\mbox{ for all }k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\}.

Because our characterization is entirely algebraic, we provide an algorithm (§5.2) based on Theorem 1.6 to determine ωm,α\omega_{m,\alpha}, which has been implemented in the computer algebra system Macaulay2 [26], see [33].

As a first illustration of the general theory, we readily reveal some deeper consequences starting from the following simple identity:

∂x⋅fs=s⋅1f∂f∂x⋅fs.\partial_{x}\cdot f^{s}=s\cdot\frac{1}{f}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot f^{s}.

By Theorem 1.6, this identity immediately yields ωm,0≤1\omega_{m,0}\leq 1 for the element m:⁣=1f∂f∂xm\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\frac{1}{f}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}. Furthermore, if m∉𝒪Xm\not\in\mathcal{O}_{X}, then ωm,0=1\omega_{m,0}=1. This is already powerful: it immediately recovers Saito’s result IC{f=0}=WdimX+1(𝒪X)f/𝒪X\mathrm{IC}_{\{f=0\}}=W_{\dim X+1}(\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f}/\mathcal{O}_{X} [46, (4.5.9)], and provides a simple argument for the classical Barlet–Kashiwara theorem [1, Theorem 1.1] in the hypersurface case, which states that the class [m][m] lies in IC{f=0}\mathrm{IC}_{\{f=0\}}.

We finish this section by a comparison with Theorem 1.3: even though the element pm,α​(s)pm,α​(−α)​m​fs\frac{p_{m,\alpha}(s)}{p_{m,\alpha}(-\alpha)}mf^{s} lifts m​f−αmf^{-\alpha} via the map in (3), in general it may not serve as the correct lift of m​f−α∈Wq+ωm,α​(ℳ⋅f−α)mf^{-\alpha}\in W_{q+\omega_{m,\alpha}}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) under the sequence in Theorem 1.2. The key insight motivating the definition of ωm,α\omega_{m,\alpha} is that we do not actually need the exact functional equation (1); rather, it suffices to consider its “modulo (s+α)ℓ(s+\alpha)^{\ell}” variant (4). It is precisely this relaxed condition that captures the weight level of m​f−αmf^{-\alpha}.

Though we have a precise algorithm determining the weight level ω\omega, the mod-equations yielding them are conceptually more mysterious than the classical Bernstein–Sato equations yielding ν\nu, and the algorithmic determination of ω\omega often takes longer than the invariants ν\nu. Moreover, the invariants ν\nu are more accessible and rigid in the sense that they are bound to some inequalities that make them easier to control (e.g. see Proposition 3.28, and examples in Section 6.5). Thus, we believe Question 1.4 to be particularly relevant.

1.3. Applications to singularity invariants

In the remaining sections, we deduce several applications to classical invariants of singularities. Let f:X→ℂf:X\to\mathbb{C} be a non-invertible regular function on a smooth algebraic variety XX.

1.3.1. Nilpotency index

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a simple holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module such that ℳ:⁣=𝒮f≠0\mathcal{M}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\mathcal{S}_{f}\neq 0, and fix α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}. A fundamental invariant of singularities is the nilpotency index nαn_{\alpha}, defined as the smallest integer nn such that (s+α)n⋅grVα​ι+​ℳ=0(s+\alpha)^{n}\cdot\mathrm{gr}^{\alpha}_{V}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}=0. While this invariant has been extensively studied in the literature (see e.g. [22]), a major computational difficulty remains: even in the simplest geometric setting where 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X} and ff has isolated singularities, there is no general, explicit formula for nαn_{\alpha}.

We solve this problem by expressing nαn_{\alpha} via multiplicities of bb-functions. Recall from Theorem 1.1 that the invariant νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha} arises as the stabilization of these multiplicities. We also have the monotonicity relation νm,α≤νm,α+1\nu_{m,\alpha}\leq\nu_{m,\alpha+1} (Lemma 3.25). On the other hand, [14, Corollary 2.7] shows that for any w∈Vα​ι+​ℳw\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, the multiplicity is given by

mults=−α⁡bw​(s)=min⁡{ℓ∣(s+α)ℓ​[w]=0∈grVα​ι+​ℳ}.\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{w}(s)=\min\{\ell\mid(s+\alpha)^{\ell}[w]=0\in\mathrm{gr}^{\alpha}_{V}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\}.

Applying this to w=pm,α​(s)​m​fsw=p_{m,\alpha}(s)mf^{s} and using the isomorphism grVα+1​ι+​ℳ≅grVα​ι+​ℳ\mathrm{gr}^{\alpha+1}_{V}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}\cong\mathrm{gr}^{\alpha}_{V}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, the sequence {νm,α+k}k∈ℤ≥0\{\nu_{m,\alpha+k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}} is uniformly bounded from above by nαn_{\alpha}. In particular, the limit limk→∞νm,α+k\lim_{k\to\infty}\nu_{m,\alpha+k} must exist. It turns out this limit recovers the nilpotency index.

Theorem 1.8 (Theorem 6.1).

For any 0≠m∈ℳ0\neq m\in\mathcal{M}, we have

nα=limk→∞νm,α+k,n_{\alpha}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\nu_{m,\alpha+k},

where the limit stabilizes for k≥max⁡{k0∈ℤ∣bm​(−α−k0)=0}k\geq\max\{k_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}\mid b_{m}(-\alpha-k_{0})=0\}.

As a corollary, when 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}, we can compute nαn_{\alpha} explicitly in terms of two bb-functions. Note that in this case, we can choose α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}, and nαn_{\alpha} coincides with the nilpotency index of the log monodromy operator on the nearby cycles ψf,e−2​π​i​α​ℚ\psi_{f,e^{-2\pi i\alpha}}\mathbb{Q}. Below, let bg​(s)b_{g}(s) denote the standard Bernstein-Sato polynomial for a function gg.

Corollary 1.9.

Let −β-\beta be the smallest and −γ-\gamma the largest root of bf​(s)b_{f}(s) in −α+ℤ-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}. Then

(7) nα=mults=−β/k​bfk​(s),∀k≥β−γ+1.n_{\alpha}=\underset{s=-\beta/k}{\mult}b_{f^{k}}(s),\hskip 10.00002pt\forall k\geq\beta-\gamma+1.

If ff has isolated singularities, (7) computes the maximal size among all Jordan blocks for the e−2​π​i​αe^{-2\pi i\alpha}-eigenspaces of the local monodromy on the cohomology of the Milnor fiber. Furthermore, Corollary 1.9 immediately gives the following bounds for nαn_{\alpha} in terms of bf​(s)b_{f}(s) (see Corollary 6.2), based on the sharper bounds in Proposition 3.28:

(8) mults=−α⁡bf​(s)≤nα≤∑α′∈α+ℤmults=−α′⁡bf​(s),\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{f}(s)\leq n_{\alpha}\leq\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}\in\,\alpha+\mathbb{Z}}\mult_{s=-\alpha^{\prime}}b_{f}(s),

which might be known to some experts; for example, it can be also deduced from Saito’s GG-filtration [48]. The upper bound in (8) is sharp and can be achieved—for example, if f=detf=\mathrm{det} on the space XX of square matrices and α=0\alpha=0. However, we can establish a strict lower bound whenever α∈ℤ≥2\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}.

Proposition 1.10 (Proposition 6.3).

If α∈ℤ≥2\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}, then ν1,α>mults=−α⁡bf​(s)\nu_{1,\alpha}>\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{f}(s).

In particular, since nα≥ν1,αn_{\alpha}\geq\nu_{1,\alpha} by Theorem 1.8, we have nα>mults=−α⁡bf​(s)n_{\alpha}>\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{f}(s).

To wrap up the discussion, we note a similar stabilization phenomenon for the weight levels. By Proposition 5.19, the length of the weight filtration on ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} coincides with the nilpotency index nαn_{\alpha}, thus we have ωm,α≤nα\omega_{m,\alpha}\leq n_{\alpha}. The weight level of m​f−α−kmf^{-\alpha-k} inside ℳ⋅f−α−k\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha-k} also stabilizes, i.e.,

with the limit achieved at the same k≥max⁡{k0∈ℤ∣bm​(−α−k0)=0}k\geq\max\{k_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}\mid b_{m}(-\alpha-k_{0})=0\} (Theorem 6.1). Further, in the maximal case we do have equality between ν\nu and ω\omega (see Proposition 5.19):

(9) ωm,α=nα​ if and only if ​νm,α=nα.\omega_{m,\alpha}=n_{\alpha}\,\,\mbox{ if and only if }\,\,\nu_{m,\alpha}=n_{\alpha}.

1.3.2. Archimedean zeta function

Suppose X⊆ℂnX\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n} is an open domain, and ff holomorphic on XX. Recall from [14] the Archimedean zeta function ZfZ_{f} is defined as the distribution that maps a compactly supported smooth function φ\varphi on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} (with support contained in XX) to Zf​(φ,s)Z_{f}(\varphi;s), to the meromorphic extension of

s↦∫X|f|2​s​φ​𝑑μ​(x),Re(s)>0,s\mapsto\int_{X}|f|^{2s}\varphi\,\,d\mu(x),\hskip 10.00002pt\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(s)>0,

where d​μ​(x)d\mu(x) is the Lebesgue measure. A value s0s_{0} is a pole of ZfZ_{f} if it is a pole of Zf​(φ,s)Z_{f}(\varphi;s) for some test function φ\varphi. For any α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}, the pole order of ZfZ_{f} at s=−αs=-\alpha is defined as ords=−αZf:⁣=max𝜑ords=−αZf(φ;s)\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{f}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\underset{\varphi}{\max}\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{f}(\varphi;s). A classical result of Bernstein [7] states that for every pole −α-\alpha of ZfZ_{f} with α∈ℚ>0\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}, one has

(10) ords=−α​Zf≤mults=−α​∏i=0rbf​(s+i),for r≫0.\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{f}\leq\underset{s=-\alpha}{\mult}\prod_{i=0}^{r}b_{f}(s+i),\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{for $r\gg 0$}.

Conversely, Barlet [3] proved that for any root −α-\alpha of bf​(s)b_{f}(s), there exists some integer k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that −α−k-\alpha-k is a pole of ZfZ_{f}.

One of the remaining difficulties is to explicitly determine the shift kk and the corresponding pole orders, which pertain to Gelfand’s original problem [25]. In recent joint work with Davis [14, Theorem 1.5], the authors established an effective bound for kk using the theory of mixed Hodge modules. However, since this bound depends on the Hodge filtration on grVα​ι+​𝒪X\mathrm{gr}^{\alpha}_{V}\iota_{+}\mathcal{O}_{X}, it is not so easy to compute in practice. Furthermore, outside the case of the minimal exponent, the precise pole orders remained undetermined.

We overcome this difficulty and determine the precise shifts as well as pole orders, depending only on explicit data from bf​(s)b_{f}(s). This effectively solves Gelfand’s problem up to finitely many (explicit) exceptions. First, in Lemma 6.4, we improve the bound (10) to the following, in view of (2),

(11) ords=−α​Zf≤ν1,α≤nα.\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{f}\leq\nu_{1,\alpha}\leq n_{\alpha}.

Furthermore, if −α-\alpha is a pole of ZfZ_{f}, then −α−1-\alpha-1 is also a pole of ZfZ_{f} with ords=−α​Zf≤ords=−α−1​Zf\underset{s=-\alpha}{\mathrm{ord}}Z_{f}\leq\underset{s=-\alpha-1}{\mathrm{ord}}Z_{f}. It follows that the sequence {ords=−α−k​Zf}k∈ℤ≥0\{\mathrm{ord}_{s=-\alpha-k}Z_{f}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}} has a limit. We determine when this limit is achieved and compute its value.

Theorem 1.11.

Let α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q} such that bf​(−α)=0b_{f}(-\alpha)=0. If k≥max⁡{k0∈ℤ≥0∣bf​(−α−k0)=0}k\geq\max\{k_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\mid b_{f}(-\alpha-k_{0})=0\}, then −α−k-\alpha-k is a pole of ZfZ_{f} and

ords=−α−k​Zf=ν1,α+k=nα.\underset{s=-\alpha-k}{\mathrm{ord}}Z_{f}=\nu_{1,\alpha+k}=n_{\alpha}.

In particular, we have limk→∞ords=−α−k​Zf=nα\lim_{k\to\infty}\,\underset{s=-\alpha-k}{\mathrm{ord}}Z_{f}=n_{\alpha}.

If ff has only isolated singularities, a similar relation between pole orders and nilpotency index was previously obtained by Barlet–Maire asymptotically [2]. Furthermore, for arbitrary α\alpha we improve (11) in terms of the weight level ω1,α\omega_{1,\alpha}, see Proposition 6.8.

To wrap up, in the case of quasi-homogeneous polynomial of isolated singularities, pole orders of ZfZ_{f} are studied by Loeser [32]. Building on his work and using our mechanism of ν\nu, we can completely determine the pole orders in this case.

Proposition 1.12 (Corollary 6.23, Corollary 6.25).

If ff is a quasi-homogeneous polynomial with isolated singularities, then for every α∈ℚ>0\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0} we have

ords=−α⁡Z1=ν1,α=ω1,α.\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}=\nu_{1,\alpha}=\omega_{1,\alpha}.

Furthermore, we have

ω1,α={0, if ​bf​(s)​ has no roots in −α+ℤ≥0;1, if either ​α∈ℤ≥1​ and ​b~f​(s)​ has no roots in −α+ℤ≥0, or ​α∉ℤ​ and ​bf​(s)​ has roots in −α+ℤ≥0;2, if ​α∈ℤ≥1​ and ​b~f​(s)​ has a root in −α+ℤ≥0.\omega_{1,\alpha}=\begin{cases}0,\mbox{ if }b_{f}(s)\mbox{ has no roots in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0};\\ 1,\mbox{ if either }\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\mbox{ and }\tilde{b}_{f}(s)\mbox{ has no roots in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\\ \quad\mbox{ or }\alpha\notin\mathbb{Z}\mbox{ and }b_{f}(s)\mbox{ has roots in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0};\\ 2,\mbox{ if }\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\mbox{ and }\tilde{b}_{f}(s)\mbox{ has a root in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.\\ \end{cases}

We want to emphasize that the bound given by ν\nu in (11) significantly improves Bernstein’s bound (10) on order of poles. In the case of quasi-homogeneous isolated singularities, when mults=−α⁡bf​(s)=1\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{f}(s)=1 for some α∈ℤ≥2\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2} and mults=−1⁡bf​(s)=2\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s)=2, then (10) only gives ords=−α​Zf≤3\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{f}\leq 3, but by above ords=−α​Zf=ν1,α=2\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{f}=\nu_{1,\alpha}=2 and also n0=2n_{0}=2 by Proposition 6.22.

1.3.3. Further applications

Let ff be an algebraic function on a smooth complex algebraic variety XX defining an irreducible hypersurface D:⁣=div(f)D\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\mathrm{div}(f). We denote by bf​(s)b_{f}(s) the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of ff.

A classical problem is to understand the explicit algebraic structure of the intersection 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module ICD\mathrm{IC}_{D}. While abstract 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module characterizations of ICD\mathrm{IC}_{D} exist, determining precisely which elements—such as the class of f−1f^{-1}—actually belong to ICD\mathrm{IC}_{D} remains a nontrivial problem.

We apply our bb-function invariants to overcome this difficulty. First, let xx be a coordinate direction on XX such that the element m=∂f∂x⋅f−1m=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot f^{-1} does not lie in 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}. We show (Proposition 6.16) that νm,0=1\nu_{m,0}=1, which implies, in particular, again that [m]∈ICD[m]\in\mathrm{IC}_{D}. It is natural to push the method further to determine exactly when the class of f−1f^{-1} itself lies in ICD\mathrm{IC}_{D}. Torrelli [53, Remark 4.4] asked whether one has an equivalence

(12) mults=−1⁡bf​(s)=1⟺[f−1]∈ICD.\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s)=1\Longleftrightarrow[f^{-1}]\in\mathrm{IC}_{D}.

In loc. cit., Torrelli proved (12) under the assumption that 𝒟X⋅f−1=(𝒪X)f\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-1}=(\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f}. We resolve his question by giving criterion for when the equivalence holds and does not hold. Furthermore, we significantly generalize his result (see Remark 6.20).

Theorem 1.13.

With the setup above, the following hold.

  1. (a)

    The `​`⇒"``\Rightarrow" part of (12) always holds: if mults=−1⁡bf​(s)=1\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s)=1, then [f−1]∈ICD[f^{-1}]\in\mathrm{IC}_{D}.

  2. (b)

    Assume either that ords=−1​Zf=mults=−1⁡bf​(s)\mathrm{ord}_{s=-1}Z_{f}=\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s) or that the nilpotency index satisfies n1=mults=−1⁡bf​(s)n_{1}=\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s), then the `​`⇐"``\Leftarrow" part of (12) holds, i.e.,

    mults=−1⁡bf​(s)>1⟹[f−1]∉ICD.\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s)>1\Longrightarrow[f^{-1}]\notin\mathrm{IC}_{D}.
  3. (c)

    There exists a polynomial hh such that the `​`⇐"``\Leftarrow" part of (12) does not hold.

    More precisely, let X=ℂnX=\mathbb{C}^{n} and g⁡(y)g(y) be a polynomial on ℂm\mathbb{C}^{m} with variables disjoint from f⁡(x)f(x). Suppose h⁡(x,y)=f⁡(x)+g⁡(y)h(x,y)=f(x)+g(y) is an irreducible polynomial on ℂn+m\mathbb{C}^{n+m}, and that the following is satisfied (e.g. if gg is quasi-homogeneous):

    Sing⁡(h−1​(0))=Sing⁡(f−1​(0))×Sing⁡(g−1​(0)).{\mathrm{Sing}}(h^{-1}(0))={\mathrm{Sing}}(f^{-1}(0))\times{\mathrm{Sing}}(g^{-1}(0)).

    and assume that there exists a unique pair of roots of bf​(s)b_{f}(s) and bg​(s)b_{g}(s), respectively, whose sum equals −1-1, say (−c,−(1−c))(-c,-(1-c)) with c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), and that both roots are simple. Then mults=−1⁡bh​(s)=2\mult_{s=-1}b_{h}(s)=2 and

    f−c∈𝒟X⋅f1−c⟹[h−1]∈ICh=0.f^{-c}\in\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{1-c}\Longrightarrow[h^{-1}]\in\mathrm{IC}_{h=0}.

In particular, using (c) we produce a counterexample to the equivalence (12), see Example 6.19. Furthermore, Theorem 1.13(b) generalizes some known results in the literature. Assume that −1-1 is the largest root of bf​(s)b_{f}(s). Then lct⁡(f)=1\mathrm{lct}(f)=1, and it is known in this case that ords=−1​Zf=mults=−1⁡bf​(s)\mathrm{ord}_{s=-1}Z_{f}=\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s) (see [14, Theorem 1.1] for example, and the discussion below it). Hence, it follows from Theorem 1.13(b) that the `​`⇐"``\Leftarrow" part of (12) holds. The lct⁡(f)=1\mathrm{lct}(f)=1 case can be seen alternatively by combining results in [47], [40], [42].

In order to prove part (c) above, in §5.5 we develop several Thom–Sebastiani-type results related to ν\nu and ω\omega. We highlight the following result, based on Euler-homogeneity, a condition analogous to the one in [48, Theorem 0.8].

Suppose 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a simple 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module. For any m∈𝒮m\in\mathcal{S} and γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}, set ν~m,γ=max⁡{νm,γ−1, 0}\tilde{\nu}_{m,\gamma}=\max\{\nu_{m,\gamma}-1,\,0\}, if γ∈ℤ≥1\gamma\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, and ν~m,γ=νm,γ\tilde{\nu}_{m,\gamma}=\nu_{m,\gamma} otherwise.

Theorem 1.14.

Let f,gf,g be functions on smooth algebraic varieties X,YX,Y, respectively, and consider h=f+gh=f+g on X×YX\times Y. Let 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} and 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} be simple holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}- and 𝒟Y\mathscr{D}_{Y}-modules underlying (complex) Hodge modules, and 𝒮=𝒮1⊠𝒮2\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{1}\boxtimes\mathcal{S}_{2}, such that (𝒮1)f,(𝒮2)g,𝒮h(\mathcal{S}_{1})_{f},(\mathcal{S}_{2})_{g},\mathcal{S}_{h} are non-zero. Assume there exists a vector field χ\chi on YY such that χ⋅g=g\chi\cdot g=g. Let mi∈𝒮im_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{i} such that χ⋅m2=c⋅m2\chi\cdot m_{2}=c\cdot m_{2}, for some c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}, and set m=m1⊠m2m=m_{1}\boxtimes m_{2}. Then for any γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R} we have

ν~m,γ=maxα+β=γν~m1,α≠0≠ν~m2,β⁡{ν~m1,α+ν~m2,β−1}.\tilde{\nu}_{m,\gamma}=\!\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha+\beta=\gamma\\ \tilde{\nu}_{m_{1},\alpha}\neq 0\neq\tilde{\nu}_{m_{2},\beta}\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\!\{\tilde{\nu}_{m_{1},\alpha}+\tilde{\nu}_{m_{2},\beta}-1\}.

We note that the inequality ≤\leq above always holds (see Corollary 5.31), in contrast with the multiplicities of roots of (reduced) Bernstein–Sato polynomials, see [48, Example 4.8]. In this sense, the invariants ν\nu behave better than the multiplicities of roots: for example, the failure of [48, Theorem 0.8] beyond the Euler-homogeneous case as in [48, Example 4.8] is rectified by working with ν\nu instead, so that in the same example we have equality above for all γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R} (see Example 5.34 with mi=1m_{i}=1).

Next, we discuss a question of Walther. Let Jac⁡(f)⊆𝒪X\mathrm{Jac}(f)\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{X} be the ideal generated by ff and its partial derivatives. In [54], the following ideal is considered for any polynomial q⁡(s)∈ℂ⁡[s]q(s)\in\mathbb{C}[s]:

𝔞f,q⁡(s)={g∈𝒪X∣q⁡(s)⋅g​fs∈𝒟X​[s]​fs+1}.\mathfrak{a}_{f,q(s)}=\{g\in\mathcal{O}_{X}\mid q(s)\cdot gf^{s}\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]f^{s+1}\}.

One can show that

𝔞f,s+1=𝒪X∩(ann𝒟X​[s]​(fs)+𝒟X​[s]⋅Jac⁡(f)).\mathfrak{a}_{f,s+1}=\mathcal{O}_{X}\cap\left(\mathrm{ann}_{\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]}(f^{s})+\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]\cdot\mathrm{Jac}(f)\right).

Clearly, Jac⁡(f)⊆𝔞f,s+1\mathrm{Jac}(f)\subseteq\mathfrak{a}_{f,s+1}. Walther asked whether the two ideals are always equal [54, Question 1.4]. We prove the following:

Theorem 1.15.

Assume D=div⁡(f)D=\mathrm{div}(f) is reduced. Then we have

𝔞f,s+1⊆adj⁡(X,D)∩Jac⁡(f).\mathfrak{a}_{f,s+1}\subseteq\mathrm{adj}(X,D)\cap\sqrt{\mathrm{Jac}(f)}.

To finish this subsection, we discuss the question of Budur–Walther (see [52]), which asks when 𝒟X⋅f−α≠𝒟X⋅f−α+1\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha}\neq\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha+1} under the assumption bf​(−α)=0b_{f}(-\alpha)=0. While the question has a negative answer in general [52] (which Theorem 1.13(c) relies on), the following provides a result in the affirmative, see Corollary 6.9.

Corollary 1.16.

If ν1,α−1<ν1,α\nu_{1,\alpha-1}<\nu_{1,\alpha} and ords=−α​Zf=ν1,α\underset{s=-\alpha}{\mathrm{ord}}Z_{f}=\nu_{1,\alpha}, then 𝒟X⋅f−α≠𝒟X⋅f−α+1\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha}\neq\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha+1}.

Note that the condition ν1,α−1<ν1,α\nu_{1,\alpha-1}<\nu_{1,\alpha} is satisfied whenever bf​(−α)=0b_{f}(-\alpha)=0 and bf​(−α+k)≠0b_{f}(-\alpha+k)\neq 0 for any k∈ℤ>0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, as in such case ν1,α−1=0\nu_{1,\alpha-1}=0 and ν1,α=mults=−α⁡bf​(s)\nu_{1,\alpha}=\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{f}(s).

2. VV-filtrations and mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules

In this section, let XX be a smooth complex algebraic variety. We review some basic facts about the VV-filtrations and weight filtrations of mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules.

2.1. Recollection of VV-filtrations

Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be a coherent left 𝒟X{\mathscr{D}}_{X}-module. Suppose D⊆XD\subseteq X is a smooth divisor. We fix a local equation t=0t=0 for DD and a vector field ∂t\partial_{t} such that [∂t,t]=1[\partial_{t},t]=1. The VV-filtration of 𝒟X{\mathscr{D}}_{X} is the decreasing ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-indexed filtration given by

Vn​𝒟X={P∈𝒟X∣P​tm∈(tm+n)​ for all ​m≥0}.V^{n}{\mathscr{D}}_{X}=\{P\in{\mathscr{D}}_{X}\mid Pt^{m}\in(t^{m+n})\text{ for all }m\geq 0\}.

In this paper, unless otherwise specified, we work with ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-indexed VV-filtrations. We endow ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with the lexicographic ordering: α<β\alpha<\beta if and only if Re(α)<Re(β)\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(\alpha)<\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(\beta) or, if Re(α)=Re(β)\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(\alpha)=\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(\beta), then Im(α)<Im(β)\mathop{{\mathrm{Im}}}(\alpha)<\mathop{{\mathrm{Im}}}(\beta).

Definition 2.1.

A VV-filtration on ℳ{\mathcal{M}} along DD is a ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-indexed filtration {Vα​ℳ}α∈ℂ\{V^{\alpha}{\mathcal{M}}\}_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}} satisfying the following properties:

  1. (1)

    V∙​ℳV^{\bullet}{\mathcal{M}} is decreasing, Vα−ϵ​ℳ=Vα​ℳV^{\alpha-\epsilon}{\mathcal{M}}=V^{\alpha}{\mathcal{M}} for ϵ∈ℂ\epsilon\in\mathbb{C} with ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 and |ϵ|≪1|\epsilon|\ll 1 (i.e., left continuous), and, locally on XX, there exists a finite set A⊆ℂA\subseteq\mathbb{C} such that Vα+ϵ​ℳ=Vα​ℳV^{\alpha+\epsilon}\mathcal{M}=V^{\alpha}\mathcal{M} for α∉A+ℤ\alpha\not\in A+\mathbb{Z}.

  2. (2)

    The filtration V∙​ℳV^{\bullet}\mathcal{M} is good over V∙​𝒟XV^{\bullet}\mathscr{D}_{X}, i.e., it is exhaustive, satisfies Vn​𝒟X⋅Vα​ℳ⊆Vα+n​ℳV^{n}{\mathscr{D}}_{X}\cdot V^{\alpha}{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq V^{\alpha+n}{\mathcal{M}} for all α∈ℂ,n∈ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{C},n\in\mathbb{Z}, each Vα​ℳV^{\alpha}{\mathcal{M}} is a coherent V0​𝒟XV^{0}{\mathscr{D}}_{X}-module, and there exists, locally on XX, a finite set of indices {αi∈ℂ}i∈I\{\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{C}\}_{i\in I} such that

    Vα​ℳ=∑n∈ℤ,i∈In+αi≥αVn​𝒟X⋅Vαi​ℳ,for all α∈ℂ.V^{\alpha}\mathcal{M}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\mathbb{Z},i\in I\\ n+\alpha_{i}\geq\alpha\end{subarray}}V^{n}\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot V^{\alpha_{i}}\mathcal{M},\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{for all $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$}.

    In particular, the operator t:Vα​ℳ→Vα+1​ℳt:V^{\alpha}{\mathcal{M}}\to V^{\alpha+1}{\mathcal{M}} is an isomorphism for Re​(α)≫0\textrm{Re}(\alpha)\gg 0.

  3. (3)

    For each α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}, the operator (−∂tt+α)(-\partial_{t}t+\alpha) is nilpotent on grVαℳ:⁣=Vαℳ/V>αℳ\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{\alpha}{\mathcal{M}}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}V^{\alpha}\mathcal{M}/V^{>\alpha}\mathcal{M}, where V>αℳ:⁣=∪α′>αVα′ℳV^{>\alpha}\mathcal{M}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\cup_{\alpha^{\prime}>\alpha}V^{\alpha^{\prime}}\mathcal{M}.

It is known [29] that if ℳ\mathcal{M} is holonomic, then the VV-filtration on ℳ\mathcal{M} along DD exists and is unique; see also [44, Proposition 2.3.2]. In connection to mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules, we also need to work with ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-indexed VV-filtrations.

Definition 2.2.

An ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-indexed VV-filtration on ℳ{\mathcal{M}} along DD is a filtration {Vβ​ℳ}β∈ℝ\{V^{\beta}{\mathcal{M}}\}_{\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}} satisfying the following properties:

  2. (2)

    The filtration V∙​ℳV^{\bullet}\mathcal{M} is good over V∙​𝒟XV^{\bullet}\mathscr{D}_{X}; that is, it is exhaustive, Vn​𝒟X⋅Vβ​ℳ⊆Vβ+n​ℳV^{n}{\mathscr{D}}_{X}\cdot V^{\beta}{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq V^{\beta+n}{\mathcal{M}} for all β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} and n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, each Vβ​ℳV^{\beta}{\mathcal{M}} is a coherent V0​𝒟XV^{0}{\mathscr{D}}_{X}-module, and there exists, locally on XX, a finite set of indices {βi∈ℝ}i∈I\{\beta_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}\}_{i\in I} such that

    Vβ​ℳ=∑n∈ℤ,i∈In+βi≥βVn​𝒟X⋅Vβi​ℳ,for all β∈ℝ.V^{\beta}\mathcal{M}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\mathbb{Z},i\in I\\ n+\beta_{i}\geq\beta\end{subarray}}V^{n}\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot V^{\beta_{i}}\mathcal{M},\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{for all $\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}$}.

    In particular, the operator t:Vβ​ℳ→Vβ+1​ℳt:V^{\beta}{\mathcal{M}}\to V^{\beta+1}{\mathcal{M}} is an isomorphism for β≫0\beta\gg 0.

  3. (3)

    For each β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}, there exist, locally on XX, finitely many indices α1,…,αk∈ℂ\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\in\mathbb{C} with Re(αi)=β\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(\alpha_{i})=\beta such that the operator ∏i=1k(−∂tt+αi)\prod_{i=1}^{k}(-\partial_{t}t+\alpha_{i}) acts by zero on grVβ​ℳ=Vβ​ℳ/V>β​ℳ\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{\beta}{\mathcal{M}}=V^{\beta}\mathcal{M}/V^{>\beta}\mathcal{M}.

Lemma 2.3.

A coherent 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module ℳ\mathcal{M} admits a VV-filtration along DD if and only if it admits an ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-indexed VV-filtration along DD.

Proof.

Suppose first that {Vα​ℳ}α∈ℂ\{V^{\alpha}\mathcal{M}\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{C}} is a ℂ\mathbb{C}-indexed VV-filtration. For β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}, define

Because 𝒮−α\mathcal{S}^{-\alpha} underlies the pure imaginary 𝒯α\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}, by the discussion above, λ=1\lambda=1 is generic with respect to the KMS spectrum KMS​(𝒯α,f)\textrm{KMS}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha},f). In particular, the sequence (18) underlies the exact sequence of mixed twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules, i.e. by setting λ=1\lambda=1,

0→𝒯α→𝒯α[∗D]→𝒯α[∗D]/𝒯α→0.0\to\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\to\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}[\ast D]\to\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}[\ast D]/\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\to 0.

Note that 𝒯α\mathcal{T}_{\alpha} is a pure twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module of weight qq, and the weight filtration of 𝒯α[∗D]\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}[\ast D] starts at qq. By the strictness of weight filtrations, the semisimplicity of Wq​(ℳ⋅f−α)W_{q}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) and the fact that 𝒮−α\mathcal{S}^{-\alpha} is the unique simple submodule of ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}, we have Wq​(ℳ⋅f−α)=𝒮−αW_{q}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\mathcal{S}^{-\alpha}.

For (17), denote by U∙​ι+​ℳU^{\bullet}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} the ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-indexed VV-filtration along {t=0}\{t=0\}. Lemma 2.3 implies that grVα​ι+​ℳ\mathrm{gr}^{\alpha}_{V}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} is the generalized α\alpha-eigenspace of grURe​(α)​ι+​ℳ\mathrm{gr}^{\textrm{Re}(\alpha)}_{U}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} for the action of ∂tt\partial_{t}t. ψ~f,uα𝒯0,uα:⁣=(−Re(α),−12Im(α)).\widetilde{\psi}_{f,u_{\alpha}}\mathcal{T}_{0},\hskip 10.00002ptu_{\alpha}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\left(-\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(\alpha),\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}\mathop{{\mathrm{Im}}}(\alpha)\right).

3. Power bb-functions and pp-functions

We introduce power bb-functions and pp-functions, and establish some fundamental properties. Let ff be an algebraic function on a smooth complex algebraic variety XX (or holomorphic function on a complex manifold), ι:X→X×ℂt\iota:X\to X\times\mathbb{C}_{t} the graph embedding, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module such that ff acts bijectively.

for some P⁡(s,t)∈𝒟X​⟨s,t⟩P(s,t)\in\mathscr{D}_{X}\langle s,t\rangle. If w=p⁡(s)​m​fsw=p(s)mf^{s}, set bp⁡(s)​m(s):⁣=bw(s)b_{p(s)m}(s)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}b_{w}(s) and we can choose P​(s)∈𝒟X​[s]P(s)\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s] in (19).

For the last three results of this subsection, we assume ℳ=𝒮f\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{S}_{f}, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a simple holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module.

Lemma 3.11.

For any w,w′∈ℳ⁡[s]​fsw,w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s}, there exists an operator P∈𝒟X​⟨s,t⟩P\in\mathscr{D}_{X}\langle s,t\rangle such that

Proof.

Since ι+​(ℳ/𝒮)\iota_{+}(\mathcal{M}/\mathcal{S}) supports on {t=0}\{t=0\}, there exists an a∈ℤ≥0a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that ta⋅w,ta⋅w′∈ι+​𝒮t^{a}\cdot w,t^{a}\cdot w^{\prime}\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{S}. Applying P3P_{3} to (29) immediately gives (28). ∎

For m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} and α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, if bm​(s)b_{m}(s) has no roots in −α−ℤ>0-\alpha-\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, then 𝒟X⋅(m​f−α)=ℳ⋅f−α\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot(mf^{-\alpha})=\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}.

For any w,w1,w2∈ℳ⁡[s]​fsw,w_{1},w_{2}\in\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s} and Q∈𝒟X​[s]Q\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s], there exists k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that

3.3. pp-functions

Recall that ℳ\mathcal{M} is a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module such that ff acts bijectively. The notion of the pp-function of an element m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} is introduced in [34, Definition 2.11]. In this section, we provide a systematic treatment of its properties. Below, we will use the isomorphism ℳ⁡[s]​fs≅ι+​ℳ\mathcal{M}[s]f^{s}\cong\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} from (13) throughout.

Lemma 3.14.

For a non-zero w∈ι+​ℳw\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} and α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, the set

Iw,α:⁣={p(s)∈ℂ[s]∣bp⁡(s)​w has no roots >−α}I_{w,\alpha}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{p(s)\in\mathbb{C}[s]\mid\textrm{$b_{p(s)w}$ has no roots $>-\alpha$}\}

forms a non-zero ideal in ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s].

Proof.

By Theorem 3.2, Im,αI_{m,\alpha} can be defined via the intersection:

(30) ℂ⁡[s]​w∩Vα​ι+​ℳ=Iw,α⋅w.\mathbb{C}[s]w\,\cap\,V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}=I_{w,\alpha}\cdot w.

From this it is clear that Iw,αI_{w,\alpha} is an ideal. To see that it is non-zero, let β∈ℂ\beta\in\mathbb{C} such that w∈Vβ​ι+​ℳw\in V^{\beta}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}. We construct a non-zero element p⁡(s)∈Iw,αp(s)\in I_{w,\alpha} inductively on β\beta. If β≥α\beta\geq\alpha, then we can pick p⁡(s)=1p(s)=1. Otherwise, Let ν:=mults=−β⁡bw​(s)\nu:=\mult_{s=-\beta}b_{w}(s). By (21), we have w′:=(s+β)ν​w∈V>β​ι+​ℳ=Vβ′​ι+​ℳw^{\prime}:=(s+\beta)^{\nu}w\in V^{>\beta}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}=V^{\beta^{\prime}}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, for some β′>β\beta^{\prime}>\beta. By the induction hypothesis, there exists a non-zero p′​(s)∈ℂ​[s]p^{\prime}(s)\in\mathbb{C}[s] such that p′​(s)​w′∈Vα​ι+​ℳp^{\prime}(s)w^{\prime}\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}. Then p⁡(s):=(s+β)ν⋅p′​(s)p(s):=(s+\beta)^{\nu}\cdot p^{\prime}(s) is the desired polynomial. ∎

Definition 3.15.

For a non-zero w∈ι+​ℳw\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, we define the pp-function of ww with respect to α\alpha, denoted by pw,α​(s)p_{w,\alpha}(s), as the unique monic polynomial p⁡(s)∈ℂ⁡[s]p(s)\in\mathbb{C}[s] of minimal degree such that p⁡(s)​w∈Vα​ι+​ℳp(s)w\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}; i.e., (pw,α​(s))=Iw,α(p_{w,\alpha}(s))=I_{w,\alpha}, by Theorem 3.2. When w=m⋅fsw=m\cdot f^{s} with m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, we will put pm,α​(s):=pw,α​(s)p_{m,\alpha}(s):=p_{w,\alpha}(s).

The proof of Lemma 3.14 together with (21) shows the roots of pw,α​(s)p_{w,\alpha}(s) are ℤ≤0\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}-shifts of roots of bw​(s)b_{w}(s).

The following is clear since the VV-filtration is decreasing.

Lemma 3.17.

Let w∈ι+​ℳw\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}. For α≤β\alpha\leq\beta, we have pw,α​(s)|pw,β​(s)p_{w,\alpha}(s)\,\mid\,p_{w,\beta}(s).

Proposition 3.18.

For Re​(α)≫0\textrm{Re}(\alpha)\gg 0, we have bw​(s)|pw,α​(s)b_{w}(s)\,|\,p_{w,\alpha}(s).

We pick Re​(β)≫0\textrm{Re}(\beta)\gg 0 such that tk:Vβ​𝒩→Vβ+k​𝒩t^{k}:V^{\beta}\mathcal{N}\to V^{\beta+k}\mathcal{N} is an isomorphism, for any k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Then there exist an integer k0≥1k_{0}\geq 1 such that tk0⋅Pi​(t,∂t)∈V0​𝒟X×ℂ=𝒟X​⟨s,t⟩t^{k_{0}}\cdot P_{i}(t,\partial t)\in V^{0}\mathscr{D}_{X\times\mathbb{C}}=\mathscr{D}_{X}\langle s,t\rangle, for all ii. Consequently, we have

By definition, this implies that bw​(s)|pw,α0​(s)b_{w}(s)\,\mid\,p_{w,\alpha_{0}}(s). Hence, bw​(s)|pw,α​(s)b_{w}(s)\,\mid\,p_{w,\alpha}(s) for any α≥α0\alpha\geq\alpha_{0} by Lemma 3.17. ∎

Corollary 3.19.

Let w∈Vβ​ι+​ℳw\in V^{\beta}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} and set ν:=mults=−β⁡bw​(s)\nu:=\mult_{s=-\beta}b_{w}(s) and w′=(s+β)ν⋅ww^{\prime}=(s+\beta)^{\nu}\cdot w. It follows from the proof of Lemma 3.14 that we have pw,α​(s)|(s+β)ν⋅pw′,α​(s)p_{w,\alpha}(s)\,\mid(s+\beta)^{\nu}\cdot p_{w^{\prime},\alpha}(s) and w′∈V>β​ι+​ℳw^{\prime}\in V^{>\beta}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}. Lemma 3.20.

We have the following:

    For w1,w2∈ι+​ℳw_{1},w_{2}\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, we have pw1+w2,α​(s)|lcm⁡(pw1,α​(s),pw2,α​(s))p_{w_{1}+w_{2},\alpha}(s)\,\mid\,\mathrm{lcm}(p_{w_{1},\alpha}(s),p_{w_{2},\alpha}(s)).

For part (ii), since pw,α​(s)​w∈Vα​ι+​ℳp_{w,\alpha}(s)w\in V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, multiplying this by Q⁡(s)Q(s) yields the conclusion. ∎

Corollary 3.21.

We have the following:

    For w1,w2∈ι+​ℳw_{1},w_{2}\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}, any root of bw1+w2​(s)b_{w_{1}+w_{2}}(s) is a ℤ≤0\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}-shift of a root of bw1​(s)b_{w_{1}}(s) or bw2​(s)b_{w_{2}}(s).

Pick α\alpha with Re​(α)≫0\textrm{Re}(\alpha)\gg 0. By Remark 3.16, roots of pwi,α​(s)p_{w_{i},\alpha}(s) are ℤ≤0\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}-shifts of roots of bwi​(s)b_{w_{i}}(s). But by Proposition 3.18, the same is true for bw1+w2​(s)b_{w_{1}+w_{2}}(s), proving part (i). Part (ii) follows analogously using Lemma 3.20 (ii) instead. ∎

Corollary 3.22.

For a non-zero w∈ι+​ℳw\in\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} and α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, the set

I~w,α:⁣={p~(s)∈ℂ[s]∣bp~​(s)​w​(s) has no roots in −α+ℤ>0}\tilde{I}_{w,\alpha}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{\tilde{p}(s)\in\mathbb{C}[s]\mid\textrm{$b_{\tilde{p}(s)w}(s)$ has no roots in $-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$}\}

Lemma 3.25.

Proposition 3.26.

5. The weight filtration on the localization

Let XX be a smooth complex algebraic variety and ff an algebraic function on XX. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module where ff acts injectively (so that 𝒮↪𝒮f\mathcal{S}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{f}). Let α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}. 5.1. A mod bb-function description of the weight filtration

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.6. We first introduce a filtration on ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} for any ℳ\mathcal{M} holonomic with ℳ=ℳf\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_{f}.

Definition 5.1.

Remark 5.7.

Corollary 1.7 is inspired by [15, Theorem 3.1], which states that if 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies a complex Hodge module, then the weight filtration on ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha} coincides with the Jantzen filtration up to a shift. This shift property was originally established by Beilinson–Bernstein [6] for mixed sheaves over finite base fields in their work on Jantzen’s conjecture. See also [27, §4.6].

Let us mention what happens in the analytic setting, when XX is a complex analytic manifold, ff a holomorphic function, and 𝒮\mathcal{S} a simple holonomic analytic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module. The equality ℬ0​(ℳ⋅f−α)=𝒮−α\mathcal{B}_{0}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\mathcal{S}^{-\alpha} still holds, as well as

ℬℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)={m​f−α∣ωm,α≤ℓ}.\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\{mf^{-\alpha}\mid\omega_{m,\alpha}\leq\ell\}.

In fact, whenever 𝒮\mathcal{S} underlies the structure of a (purely imaginary) twistor 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module (or a complex pure Hodge module [43]) structure, the results of this section extend in the analytic setting, and Wq+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)=ℬℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}). For example, this applies to 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}. However, due to the known failure of the decomposition theorem in this setup in general, we pose the following as a challenge.

Problem 5.8.

Suppose 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a simple holonomic analytic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module, find an example where grℓℬ​(ℳ⋅f−α)\mathrm{gr}_{\ell}^{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) is not a semisimple analytic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module, with ℓ>0\ell>0.

[Test the weight level]

  2. (2)

    Compute generators of If:=Ann𝒟X​[s]​(fs)I_{f}:=\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]}(f^{s}).

  3. (3)

    Then g⋅f−α∈WdimX+ω​(ℳ⋅f−α)g\cdot f^{-\alpha}\in W_{\dim X+\omega}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) if and only if

    (s+α+k1)ω⋅g​fk1∈If+𝒟X​[s]⋅((s+α+k1)ω+1,fk1+k2).(s+\alpha+k_{1})^{\omega}\cdot gf^{k_{1}}\,\in\,I_{f}+\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]\cdot((s+\alpha+k_{1})^{\omega+1},\,f^{k_{1}+k_{2}}).
Remark 5.10.

Since W∙​(ℳ⋅f−α)≅W∙​(ℳ⋅f−(α−1))W_{\bullet}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})\cong W_{\bullet}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-(\alpha-1)}), it follows that ωm,α=ωm​fℓ,α+ℓ\omega_{m,\alpha}=\omega_{mf^{\ell},\alpha+\ell} for any ℓ\ell. We may therefore always assume m∈𝒪Xm\in\mathcal{O}_{X}.

Remark 5.11.

Computing b1​(s)b_{1}(s) is computationally expensive. To reduce computation time, one can use a priori estimates for k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} without computing b1​(s)b_{1}(s). We may assume 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, then

  1. (1)

    One can replace k1k_{1} with ⌈n−1−α⌉\lceil n-1-\alpha\rceil. By [48, Theorem 0.4], if α+k1+1≥n\alpha+k_{1}+1\geq n, then b1​(−α−k1−i)≠0b_{1}(-\alpha-k_{1}-i)\neq 0 for all i∈ℤ≥1i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, which suffices for the algorithm. For special ff, tighter bounds exist: if ff defines a central hyperplane arrangement, all roots of b1​(s)b_{1}(s) are within (−2,0)(-2,0) [50, Theorem 1], so we can set k1=⌈1−α⌉k_{1}=\lceil 1-\alpha\rceil.

Step (3) relies on the following lemma:

Lemma 5.12.

For g∈𝒪Xg\in\mathcal{O}_{X}, the weight level ωg,α\omega_{g,\alpha} is the smallest integer ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 such that

P⁡(s)​fs+k2=(s+α)ℓ​g​fs(mod(s+α)ℓ+1⋅𝒟X​[s]​fs−k1)P(s)f^{s+k_{2}}=(s+\alpha)^{\ell}gf^{s}\pmod{(s+\alpha)^{\ell+1}\cdot\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]f^{s-k_{1}}}

for some P​(s)∈𝒟X​[s]P(s)\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]. In particular, the entire relation takes place in 𝒟X​[s]​fs−k1\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]f^{s-k_{1}}.

Set m=fk2m=f^{k_{2}}. Because bm​(s)=b1​(s+k2)b_{m}(s)=b_{1}(s+k_{2}) has no roots in −α+ℤ≥0-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, Remark 5.6 implies that ωg,α\omega_{g,\alpha} is the smallest ℓ∈ℤ≥0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} satisfying an equation of the form

By our choice of k1k_{1}, we can repeatedly apply the defining equation of the Bernstein–Sato polynomial of ff to find Q​(s)∈𝒟X​[s]Q(s)\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s] and b⁡(s)∈ℂ⁡[s]b(s)\in\mathbb{C}[s] with b⁡(−α)=1b(-\alpha)=1 such that

R⁡(s)⋅fs+k2=(s+α)ℓ​g​fs+(s+α)ℓ+1​(b⁡(s)​w+c⁡(s)​g​fs)R(s)\cdot f^{s+k_{2}}=(s+\alpha)^{\ell}gf^{s}+(s+\alpha)^{\ell+1}(b(s)w+c(s)gf^{s})

for some R​(s)∈𝒟X​[s]R(s)\in\mathscr{D}_{X}[s]. Since g∈𝒪Xg\in\mathcal{O}_{X}, the claim follows. ∎

Remark 5.13.

Our algorithm 5.9 provides an easy way to produce examples ff such that 𝒟X⋅f−α=𝒟X⋅f−α+1\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha}=\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha+1} when bf​(−α)=0b_{f}(-\alpha)=0, which is a question of Budur and Walther discussed in the introduction [52]. More precisely, if α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), then f−α∈𝒟X⋅f−α+1f^{-\alpha}\in\mathscr{D}_{X}\cdot f^{-\alpha+1} if and only if f−α∈WdimX​((𝒪X)f⋅f−α)f^{-\alpha}\in W_{\dim X}\left((\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f}\cdot f^{-\alpha}\right). By Theorem 5.5, the latter is equivalent to ω1,α=0\omega_{1,\alpha}=0, which can be computed by this algorithm. This is already implemented in [16, Remark 6.9] to produce an example with small degree, compared to [52].

5.3. An approximation of the weight filtration

We study a useful approximation of Wℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)W_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) induced by νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha}.

Definition 5.14.

For ℓ∈ℤ≥0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, set 𝒩ℓ(ℳ⋅f−α):⁣={mf−α∣νm,α≤ℓ}⊆ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{mf^{-\alpha}\mid\nu_{m,\alpha}\leq\ell\}\subseteq\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}. To simplify notation, we sometimes write 𝒩ℓ\mathcal{N}_{\ell} for 𝒩ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}).

Proposition 5.15.

Let g∈𝒪Xg\in\mathcal{O}_{X} and m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}. Setting Ug:⁣={g≠0}U_{g}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{g\neq 0\}, we have

νm∣Ug,α=limk→∞νgk⋅m,α.\nu_{m_{\mid U_{g}},\alpha}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\nu_{g^{k}\cdot m,\alpha}.

Moreover, 𝒩ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)⊆Wq+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})\subseteq W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) is a quasi-coherent subsheaf of 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-modules.

Remark 5.16.

The proof that 𝒩ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) is a sheaf of 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-modules works without assuming 𝒮\mathcal{S} is simple.

Proof.

First, we show that on any affine open set, 𝒩ℓ\mathcal{N}_{\ell} is closed under addition and 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-multiplication. Let m1​f−α,m2​f−α∈𝒩ℓm_{1}f^{-\alpha},m_{2}f^{-\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}_{\ell}, and denote p(s):⁣=lcm(pm1,α(s),pm2,α(s))p(s)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\mathrm{lcm}(p_{m_{1},\alpha}(s),p_{m_{2},\alpha}(s)). By Lemmas 3.20(i) and 3.25(i), pm1+m2​(s)|p​(s)p_{m_{1}+m_{2}}(s)\mid p(s) and (s+α)∤p⁡(s)(s+\alpha)\nmid p(s). Applying Lemma 3.25(iii) to m1+m2m_{1}+m_{2} and mim_{i} yields

μp⁡(s)⋅(m1+m2),α=νm1+m2,α,μp⁡(s)⋅mi,α=νmi,α≤ℓ.\mu_{p(s)\cdot(m_{1}+m_{2}),\alpha}=\nu_{m_{1}+m_{2},\alpha},\hskip 10.00002pt\mu_{p(s)\cdot m_{i},\alpha}=\nu_{m_{i},\alpha}\leq\ell.

Since Zℓ​Vα​ι+​ℳZ_{\ell}V^{\alpha}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} is closed under addition (see Proposition 4.10), we have

μp⁡(s)⋅(m1+m2),α≤max⁡{μp⁡(s)⋅m1,α,μp⁡(s)⋅m2,α}≤ℓ.\mu_{p(s)\cdot(m_{1}+m_{2}),\alpha}\leq\max\{\mu_{p(s)\cdot m_{1},\alpha},\mu_{p(s)\cdot m_{2},\alpha}\}\leq\ell.

Consequently, (m1+m2)​f−α∈𝒩ℓ(m_{1}+m_{2})f^{-\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}_{\ell}. Clearly, 𝒩ℓ\mathcal{N}_{\ell} is also stable under scalar multiplication, making it a ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector subspace of ℳ⋅f−α\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}.

Next, let m​f−α∈𝒩ℓmf^{-\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}_{\ell} and g∈𝒪Xg\in\mathcal{O}_{X}. Lemmas 3.20(ii) and 3.25(i) show pg​m,α​(s)|pm,α​(s)p_{gm,\alpha}(s)\mid p_{m,\alpha}(s) and (s+α)∤pm,α​(s)(s+\alpha)\nmid p_{m,\alpha}(s). Applying Lemma 3.25(iii) to g⋅mg\cdot m, we find νg​m,α=μpm,α​(s)⋅g​m,α\nu_{gm,\alpha}=\mu_{p_{m,\alpha}(s)\cdot gm,\alpha}. Since pm,α​(s)​m​fs∈Zℓ​Vαp_{m,\alpha}(s)mf^{s}\in Z_{\ell}V^{\alpha}, by Proposition 4.10 again we have

μpm,α​(s)⋅g​m,α≤μpm,α​(s)⋅m,α=νm,α≤ℓ.\mu_{p_{m,\alpha}(s)\cdot gm,\alpha}\leq\mu_{p_{m,\alpha}(s)\cdot m,\alpha}=\nu_{m,\alpha}\leq\ell.

This confirms 𝒩ℓ\mathcal{N}_{\ell} is an 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-module.

Now we prove the limit equality. By the proof of Lemma 3.25(v), the sequence {νgk⋅m,α}k≥0\{\nu_{g^{k}\cdot m,\alpha}\}_{k\geq 0} is non-increasing. By Theorem 3.29, νm∣Ug,α\nu_{m_{\mid U_{g}},\alpha} is the smallest integer ν≥0\nu\geq 0 such that

(49) (s+α)ν​m​fs∈⋂i∈ℤ𝒟Ug​[s](s+α)⋅m​fs+i,(s+\alpha)^{\nu}mf^{s}\in\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathscr{D}_{U_{g}}[s]_{(s+\alpha)}\cdot mf^{s+i},

In this section, we analyze how various invariants discussed previously including pp-functions, ZZ-filtrations and weight levels ωf,α\omega_{f,\alpha} behave with respect to the Thom-Sebastiani formula.

Remark 5.33.

Note that condition (c) above is analogous to Saito’s condition in [48, Theorem 0.8] (with m1=1∈𝒮1=𝒪Xm_{1}=1\in\mathcal{S}_{1}=\mathcal{O}_{X}, m2=1∈𝒮2=𝒪Ym_{2}=1\in\mathcal{S}_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{Y}). However we don’t see a direct way to obtain one result from the other via interpreting ν\nu as multiplicities of roots of powers of Bernstein–Sato polynomials, since the sum of higher powers of ff and gg is not a power of their sum hh.

In a way, the behavior of ν\nu is better-behaved than the multiplicities of Bernstein–Sato polynomials in such Thom–Sebastiani-type results, as the following example illustrates.

Example 5.34.

We consider [48, Example 4.8], where it was shown that the reduced Bernstein–Sato polynomial b~h​(s)\tilde{b}_{h}(s) does not equal the expected convolution of b~f\tilde{b}_{f} and b~g\tilde{b}_{g}, and thus [48, Theorem 0.8] does not necessarily hold without the Euler-homogeneous assumption on gg (similar to Theorem 5.32(c) above). On the other hand, we demonstrate that on the level of ν~\tilde{\nu}, the expected equality in Theorem 5.32 does hold in this case.

Consider the Tp​q​rT_{pqr}-type isolated singularity on ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} given by:

Tp,q,r​(x,y,z)=xp+yq+zr+x​y​z, with ​p,q,r∈ℤ≥2​ such that ​1p+1q+1r<1.T_{p,q,r}(x,y,z)=x^{p}+y^{q}+z^{r}+xyz,\,\,\mbox{ with }p,q,r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}\mbox{ such that }\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{r}<1.

For f:=Tp,p,pf:=T_{p,p,p} we have (see [48, Example 4.8])

b~f​(s)=(s+1)2⋅∏i=1p−1(s+1+ip).\tilde{b}_{f}(s)=(s+1)^{2}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}(s+1+\frac{i}{p}).

Proposition 3.28 readily implies that the only non-zero ν~\tilde{\nu} are given by

  • •

    ν~fs,α=2\tilde{\nu}_{f^{s},\alpha}=2, when α∈ℤ≥1\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1};

  • •

    ν~fs,α=1\tilde{\nu}_{f^{s},\alpha}=1, when α=i/p\alpha=i/p with i∈ℤ>pi\in\mathbb{Z}_{>p} and p∤ip\nmid i.

Now take g:=Tq,q,qg:=T_{q,q,q} with gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1, and set h=f+gh=f+g. By Corollary 5.31, the only potentially non-zero ν~\tilde{\nu} are given as follows:

  • •

    ν~hs,γ≤2\tilde{\nu}_{h^{s},\gamma}\leq 2, for γ=2+i/p\gamma=2+i/p (resp. γ=2+i/q\gamma=2+i/q) with i∈ℤ>0i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} and p∤ip\nmid i (resp. OPENq∤i)q\nmid i);

  • •

    ν~hs,γ≤1\tilde{\nu}_{h^{s},\gamma}\leq 1, for γ=k+i/p+j/q\gamma=k+i/p+j/q with k∈ℤ>1k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1} and 1≤i≤p−11\leq i\leq p-1, 1≤j≤q−11\leq j\leq q-1.

  • •

    ν~hs,2+i/p=2\tilde{\nu}_{h^{s},2+i/p}=2 (resp. ν~hs,2+j/q=2\tilde{\nu}_{h^{s},2+j/q}=2) for 1≤i≤p−11\leq i\leq p-1 (resp. 1≤j≤q−11\leq j\leq q-1);

This shows that in this example we do indeed have equality for any γ\gamma (and mi=1m_{i}=1) in Corollary 5.31, in contrast with the failure of [48, Theorem 0.8] for h=f+gh=f+g.

6. Applications

In this section, we deduce several applications from the results developed in the previous sections. Let ι:X→X×ℂt\iota:X\to X\times\mathbb{C}_{t} denote the graph embedding of ff. Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module, and let V∙​ι+​ℳV^{\bullet}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} denote the ℂ\mathbb{C}-indexed VV-filtration on ι+​ℳ\iota_{+}\mathcal{M} along {t=0}\{t=0\} (Definition 2.1).

6.1. Nilpotency index

In this subsection, we prove Theorem 1.8, Corollary 1.9 and Proposition 1.10. On the other hand, because ℳ⋅f−α=ℳ⋅f−α−k\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}=\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha-k}, Corollary 5.20 implies that nα=ωm′,α=ωm,α+kn_{\alpha}=\omega_{m^{\prime},\alpha}=\omega_{m,\alpha+k}. ∎

We have μm,α≤νm,α≤nα≤∑γ∈α+ℤμm,γ\mu_{m,\alpha}\leq\nu_{m,\alpha}\leq n_{\alpha}\leq\sum_{\gamma\in\alpha+\mathbb{Z}}\mu_{m,\gamma}.

6.5. Examples

In this section, we compute several classes of examples explicitly and answer the corresponding questions raised throughout the text. Throughout the section, for simplicity we assume XX is a smooth algebraic variety and ff a regular function on XX.

6.5.1. Isolated quasihomogeneous singularities

Denote by bf​(s)b_{f}(s) the usual Bernstein-Sato polynomial of ff. Recall that b~f​(s)=bf​(s)/(s+1)\tilde{b}_{f}(s)=b_{f}(s)/(s+1) denotes the reduced Bernstein-Sato polynomial of ff.

Proposition 6.22.

Suppose ff has an isolated quasihomogeneous singularity. Then for any α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q} we have 𝒩ℓ​((𝒪X)f⋅f−α)=WdimX+ℓ​((𝒪X)f⋅f−α)\mathcal{N}_{\ell}((\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=W_{\dim X+\ell}((\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f}\cdot f^{-\alpha}). Proof.

We may assume the only singularity of ff is {0}\{0\}. Since ff is quasihomogeneous, the monodromy on the Milnor fiber FF at 00 has finite order [21, p. 19] so the corresponding monodromy on the cohomology is semisimple. Set ℳ=(𝒪X)f\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{O}_{X})_{f}.

Suppose first that α∉ℤ\alpha\not\in\mathbb{Z} with bf​(−α)=0b_{f}(-\alpha)=0. Since the singularity of ff is isolated, nαn_{\alpha} is the maximal size of a Jordan block of the monodromy on the e−2​π​i​αe^{-2\pi i\alpha}-eigenspace of Hn−1​(F,ℂ)H^{n-1}(F,\mathbb{C}). Hence nα≤1n_{\alpha}\leq 1 by the semisimplicity. In particular, by (8) we have nα=mults=−α⁡bf​(s)=1n_{\alpha}=\mult_{s=-\alpha}b_{f}(s)=1. The equality 𝒩ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)=WdimX+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=W_{\dim X+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}) then follows from Proposition 5.19.

Next, suppose α=0\alpha=0. Again because ff has an isolated singularity at {0}\{0\}, the unipotent vanishing cycles grV0​ι+​𝒪X\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{0}\iota_{+}\mathcal{O}_{X} support at {0}\{0\}, where they are identified with the eigenspace Hn−1​(F,ℂ)1H^{n-1}(F,\mathbb{C})_{1}. By above, since the monodromy on Hn−1​(F,ℂ)1H^{n-1}(F,\mathbb{C})_{1} is semisimple, the logarithm of its unipotent part, which can be identified with the action by ss on grV0​ι+​𝒪X\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{0}\iota_{+}\mathcal{O}_{X}, is zero. In other words, s⋅grV0​ι+​𝒪X=0s\cdot\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{0}\iota_{+}\mathcal{O}_{X}=0. Since s=−∂tts=-\partial_{t}t, we have

(s+1)2=(t∂t)2=t(∂tt)∂t=−ts∂t=0on grV1​ι+​𝒪X.(s+1)^{2}=(t\partial_{t})^{2}=t(\partial_{t}t)\partial_{t}=-ts\partial_{t}=0\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{on $\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{1}\iota_{+}\mathcal{O}_{X}$}.

Since V1​ι+​ℳ=V1​ι+​𝒪XV^{1}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}=V^{1}\iota_{+}\mathcal{O}_{X} and s+1=−t∂ts+1=-t\partial_{t}, it follows that

(s+1)2​grV1​ι+​ℳ=0.(s+1)^{2}\mathrm{gr}_{V}^{1}\iota_{+}\mathcal{M}=0.

Hence n0=n1≤2n_{0}=n_{1}\leq 2. Since n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1, we conclude that n0=1n_{0}=1 or 22. Thus, the equality 𝒩ℓ​(ℳ)=WdimX+ℓ​(ℳ)\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M})=W_{\dim X+\ell}(\mathcal{M}) follows from Proposition 5.19 and Remark 5.18.

Finally, there are two possibilities for integer roots. If −1-1 is the only integer root of bf​(s)b_{f}(s) with multiplicity ≤2\leq 2, then Corollary 1.9 gives n0=mults=−1⁡bf​(s)n_{0}=\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s). Otherwise, suppose bf​(s)b_{f}(s) has another integer root, say the largest such being −k-k with k∈ℤ≥2k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}. By Proposition 3.28 we have mults=−1⁡bf​(s)=ν1,1=ν1,2=⋯=ν1,k−1≤ν1,k\mult_{s=-1}b_{f}(s)=\nu_{1,1}=\nu_{1,2}=\dots=\nu_{1,k-1}\leq\nu_{1,k}. On the other hand, Proposition 6.3 implies that ν1,k≥2\nu_{1,k}\geq 2. Since ν1,k≤nk=n0\nu_{1,k}\leq n_{k}=n_{0} by Corollary 6.2, we get n0=ν1,k=2n_{0}=\nu_{1,k}=2. ∎

Note that in the proof above we implicitly obtained ν1,α\nu_{1,\alpha} for all α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}, given the well-known formula for bf​(s)b_{f}(s) (e.g. see [31, Theorem 6.18]). Furthermore, Proposition 6.22 implies that ν1,α=ω1,α\nu_{1,\alpha}=\omega_{1,\alpha}. We summarize this below.

Corollary 6.23.

With ff as above, we have

ω1,α={0, if ​bf​(s)​ has no roots in −α+ℤ≥0;1, if either ​α∈ℤ≥1​ and ​b~f​(s)​ has no roots in −α+ℤ≥0, or ​α∉ℤ​ and ​bf​(s)​ has roots in −α+ℤ≥0;2, if ​α∈ℤ≥1​ and ​b~f​(s)​ has a root in −α+ℤ≥0.\omega_{1,\alpha}=\begin{cases}0,\mbox{ if }b_{f}(s)\mbox{ has no roots in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0};\\ 1,\mbox{ if either }\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\mbox{ and }\tilde{b}_{f}(s)\mbox{ has no roots in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\\ \quad\mbox{ or }\alpha\notin\mathbb{Z}\mbox{ and }b_{f}(s)\mbox{ has roots in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0};\\ 2,\mbox{ if }\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\mbox{ and }\tilde{b}_{f}(s)\mbox{ has a root in }-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.\\ \end{cases}
Remark 6.24.

Additionally, using the computations of ν\nu we can write down the pp-functions p1,α​(s)p_{1,\alpha}(s) for all α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q} as well as formulas for the Bernstein-Sato polynomials of powers of ff.

Corollary 6.25.

With ff as above, for every α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}, then we have

ords=−α⁡Z1=ω1,α=ν1,α.\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}=\omega_{1,\alpha}=\nu_{1,\alpha}.
Proof.

By the discussion above, we have ω1,α=ν1,α\omega_{1,\alpha}=\nu_{1,\alpha}. Moreover, Lemma 6.4 gives

Moreover, whenever α∈ℤ≥1\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} and b~f​(s)\widetilde{b}_{f}(s) has a root in −α+ℤ≥0-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, the pole at s=−αs=-\alpha has order at least two.

If ω1,α=0\omega_{1,\alpha}=0, the bound (68) implies ords=−α⁡Z1=0\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}=0. If ω1,α=1\omega_{1,\alpha}=1, Corollary 6.23 implies that either α∈ℤ≥1\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, or α∉ℤ\alpha\notin\mathbb{Z} and bf​(s)b_{f}(s) has a root in −α+ℤ≥0-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. In both cases, Loeser’s theorem gives ords=−α⁡Z1≥1\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}\geq 1. Finally, if ω1,α=2\omega_{1,\alpha}=2, Corollary 6.23 gives α∈ℤ≥1\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} and a root of b~f​(s)\widetilde{b}_{f}(s) in −α+ℤ≥0-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}; hence Loeser’s theorem gives ords=−α⁡Z1≥2\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}\geq 2. Proof.

By [30], every root of bfs​(s)b_{f^{s}}(s) is negative, so fs∈V>0​ℳf^{s}\in V^{>0}\mathcal{M} by Theorem 3.2. The idea is to use Lemma 6.29 below to bound mults=−1⁡bg​fs​(s)\mult_{s=-1}b_{gf^{s}}(s). Let π:Y→X\pi:Y\to X be the iterated blowup of XX along all proper edges of 𝒜\mathcal{A} from dimensions 00 to n−1n-1, which is a log resolution of (X,div⁡(f))(X,\mathrm{div}(f)) and is an isomorphism over X∖{f=0}X\setminus\{f=0\}; this is the wonderful model associated to the maximal building set of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, see [19]. For the divisor ELE_{L}, the inequality in (71) becomes dL≥(cL−1)+(dL−eI​(L))+1d_{L}\geq(c_{L}-1)+(d_{L}-e_{I}(L))+1, equivalently eI​(L)≥cLe_{I}(L)\geq c_{L}. Since II is independent, clearly eI​(L)≤cLe_{I}(L)\leq c_{L}. Thus the divisor ELE_{L} contributes to the bound in (71) if and only if eI​(L)=cLe_{I}(L)=c_{L}. But then they must form a chain [19, §2.4, p. 472], say L1⊋⋯⊋LpL_{1}\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq L_{p}. Hence 1≤cL1<⋯<cLp≤r1\leq c_{L_{1}}<\cdots<c_{L_{p}}\leq r, so p≤rp\leq r. Remark 6.30.

Let ff define a reduced, central, and essential hyperplane arrangement in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Then, for every α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q} with α≥1\alpha\geq 1, one can show that

ords=−α⁡Z1=ω1,α=ν1,α=nα,ords=−k⁡Z1=n,∀k∈ℤ≥1.\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}=\omega_{1,\alpha}=\nu_{1,\alpha}=n_{\alpha},\hskip 10.00002pt\operatorname{ord}_{s=-k}Z_{1}=n,\hskip 10.00002pt\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}.

Indeed, by [50, Theorem 1], all roots of bfs​(s)b_{f^{s}}(s) lie in (−2,0)(-2,0), and −1-1 is a root of multiplicity nn. Fix α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q} with α≥1\alpha\geq 1. First, if bfs​(s)b_{f^{s}}(s) has no roots in −α+ℤ-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}, then nα=0n_{\alpha}=0 by Corollary 6.2. Since by Lemma 6.4, ords=−α⁡Z1≤ν1,α≤nα\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}\leq\nu_{1,\alpha}\leq n_{\alpha} and ω1,α≤ν1,α\omega_{1,\alpha}\leq\nu_{1,\alpha}, all four quantities vanish. Otherwise, let −β-\beta be the largest root of bfs​(s)b_{f^{s}}(s) in −α+ℤ-\alpha+\mathbb{Z}. Since all roots lie in (−2,0)(-2,0) and we assume α≥1\alpha\geq 1, we must have α=β+ℓ\alpha=\beta+\ell for ℓ∈ℤ≥0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Applying Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.7, we obtain

ords=−α⁡Z1=ω1,α=ν1,α=nβ=nα.\operatorname{ord}_{s=-\alpha}Z_{1}=\omega_{1,\alpha}=\nu_{1,\alpha}=n_{\beta}=n_{\alpha}.

Finally, using Remark 3.30, we obtain n1=ν1,1=mults=−1⁡bfs​(s)=nn_{1}=\nu_{1,1}=\operatorname{mult}_{s=-1}b_{f^{s}}(s)=n, which gives the second equality.

On the other hand, if α<1\alpha<1, this can be quite subtle. For example, if ff defines a central essential and indecomposable arrangement in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} and deg⁡f=d\deg f=d, one can have ords=−n/dZ1=0=ω1,n/d<1=mults=−n/dbfs(s)=ν1,n/d\operatorname{ord}_{s=-n/d}Z_{1}=0=\omega_{1,n/d}<1=\mult_{s=-n/d}b_{f^{s}}(s)=\nu_{1,n/d}. See [16, Remark 6.9] for an example.

6.5.3. Irreducible isotypic components and spherical varieties

In this section, we recast some of the results from [34] in the framework of this article. As in loc. cit., let XX be a representation of a complex connected reductive group GG, and let ff be a GG-semi-invariant function. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a simple equivariant holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module with full support on XX.

Suppose that λ\lambda is an irreducible representation of GG such that the isotypic component ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} is irreducible. Let m∈ℳλm\in\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} be a non-zero element; in this case, bm​(s)b_{m}(s) satisfies a special equation [34, Equation (2)]. In this setup, bm​(s)b_{m}(s) determines νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha} for all α\alpha, as seen in [34, Equation (5)]. In fact, the right-hand inequality in Proposition 3.28 is an equality for all α\alpha. Furthermore, [34, Theorem 1.2] can be rephrased as:

(73) ωm,α=νm,α.\omega_{m,\alpha}=\nu_{m,\alpha}.

Assuming 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}, the polynomial bm​(s)b_{m}(s) also determines the pole orders of ZmZ_{m}:

Proposition 6.31.

In the setup above, ords=−α​Zm=νm,α\underset{s=-\alpha}{\mathrm{ord}}Z_{m}=\nu_{m,\alpha}.

Proof.

Because the inequality ords=−α​Zm≤νm,α\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{m}\leq\nu_{m,\alpha} holds in general (see Lemma 6.4), it is sufficient to find a test function φ\varphi for which ords=−α​Zm​(φ,s)=νm,α\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z_{m}(\varphi;s)=\nu_{m,\alpha}.

We pick φ=exp⁡(−|x|2)\varphi=\exp(-|x|^{2}), as in [28, Theorem 6.3.1], and set Z⁡(s):=Zm​(exp⁡(−|x|2),s)Z(s):=Z_{m}(\exp(-|x|^{2});s). As in the proof of loc. cit., we obtain a functional equation (up to a constant):

(74) bm​(s)⋅Z⁡(s)=Z⁡(s+1).b_{m}(s)\cdot Z(s)=Z(s+1).

We factor bm​(s)b_{m}(s) as ∏(s+λi)\prod(s+\lambda_{i}), with λi∈ℚ\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}. We claim that there exists a non-zero constant c0∈ℝ∗c_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{*} such that

(75) Z⁡(s)=c0⋅∏iΓ⁡(s+λi).Z(s)=c_{0}\cdot\prod_{i}\Gamma(s+\lambda_{i}).

Consider the function C⁡(s)=Z⁡(s)/∏iΓ⁡(s+λi)C(s)=Z(s)/\prod_{i}\Gamma(s+\lambda_{i}). The functional equation (74) implies that C⁡(s+1)=C⁡(s)C(s+1)=C(s). Since Z⁡(s)Z(s), and thus C⁡(s)C(s), is holomorphic when Re(s)≫0\mathop{{\mathrm{Re}}}(s)\gg 0, the periodicity of C⁡(s)C(s) implies that it is holomorphic on all of ℂ\mathbb{C}. Now, the same argument as in the proof of [28, Theorem 6.3.1], mutatis mutandis, applies to show that C⁡(s)C(s) must be a non-zero constant c0c_{0}.

The formula for νm,α\nu_{m,\alpha} from [34, Equation (5)], together with (75), implies that ords=−α​Z​(s)=νm,α\underset{s=-\alpha}{\textrm{ord}}Z(s)=\nu_{m,\alpha} for all α∈ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}. ∎

Note that the result above, together with Proposition 6.8, provides a new proof of (73) based on zeta functions in the case where 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}. Additionally, it implies that Question 6.11 has a positive answer in this setup (in a strong form, since equality holds).

[34, Theorem 1.4] states that Corollary 5.23 is sharp in this setup (recall that dm,α=deg⁡pm,α​(s)d_{m,\alpha}=\deg p_{m,\alpha}(s)):

(76) The Hodge level of ​m⋅f−α​ is precisely ​dm,α.\mbox{The Hodge level of }m\cdot f^{-\alpha}\mbox{ is precisely }d_{m,\alpha}.

Now, assume XX is a smooth affine spherical variety under the action of GG, in which case a simple equivariant holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module 𝒮\mathcal{S} is automatically regular holonomic (see [34]). Then, all isotypic components of ℳ\mathcal{M} are irreducible [34, Lemma 3.6]; thus, (73) and (76) yield positive answers to Questions 1.4 and 5.28. In fact, stronger versions hold:

Corollary 6.32.

Assume that XX is a smooth affine spherical variety. Then, for all α\alpha and ℓ\ell, we have

Wq+ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)=𝒩ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α).W_{q+\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\mathcal{N}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}).

Furthermore, if 𝒮=𝒪X\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{O}_{X}, then

Fℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α)=𝒫ℓ​(ℳ⋅f−α).F_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha})=\mathcal{P}_{\ell}(\mathcal{M}\cdot f^{-\alpha}).
